q: The general formula of open-chain alkanes is:
x: Alkanes are saturated open-chain hydrocarbons with formula CₙH₂ₙ₊₂ (e.g. CH₄, C₂H₆, C₃H₈). CₙH₂ₙ is the formula of alkenes and CₙH₂ₙ₋₂ that of alkynes.

q: Ethene is prepared in the laboratory from ethanol by heating it with:
x: Concentrated sulphuric acid removes a water molecule from ethanol at about 170 °C: CH₃CH₂OH → CH₂=CH₂ + H₂O. Dilute acid at room temperature does not dehydrate ethanol.

q: The general formula of open-chain alkynes containing one triple bond is:
x: An alkyne has two fewer hydrogens than the alkene with the same number of carbons, so the formula is CₙH₂ₙ₋₂ (e.g. C₂H₂, C₃H₄). CₙH₂ₙ₊₂ is for alkanes and CₙH₂ₙ for alkenes.

q: The correct IUPAC name of CH₃CH(CH₃)CH₂CH₃ is:
x: The longest chain has four carbons (butane) and numbering from the end nearer the branch puts the methyl on C-2. 3-methylbutane numbers from the wrong end, and the other two names miss the longest chain.

q: Bromoethane is heated with alcoholic KOH. The organic product is:
x: Alcoholic KOH removes HBr from bromoethane (dehydrohalogenation): CH₃CH₂Br + KOH → CH₂=CH₂ + KBr + H₂O. Aqueous KOH would instead substitute OH for Br and give ethanol.

q: The IUPAC name of CH₃–C≡C–CH₃ is:
x: The chain has four carbons with the triple bond starting at carbon 2 from either end, so it is but-2-yne (common name dimethylacetylene). But-1-yne would have the triple bond at the end of the chain.

q: The correct IUPAC name of (CH₃)₃CCH₂CH₃ is:
x: The longest chain is four carbons, with two methyl groups on the same carbon. Numbering from the end nearer the branches gives locants 2,2, not 3,3. The other two names do not use the longest chain.

q: In the dehydrohalogenation of an alkyl halide, the hydrogen atom that is removed comes from:
o: The carbon next to the one carrying the halogen (β-carbon)
Any carbon of the chain, at random
The hydroxyl group of the alcohol solvent
x: It is a β-elimination: X leaves from the α-carbon and H from the neighbouring β-carbon, so a double bond forms between these two carbons.

q: The IUPAC name of (CH₃)₂CH–C≡CH is:
x: The longest chain containing the triple bond has four carbons, numbered from the ≡CH end so the triple bond gets locant 1; the methyl group is then on carbon 3. Numbering from the other end (2-methylbut-3-yne) gives the triple bond a higher number, which is wrong.

q: The correct IUPAC name of CH₃CH₂CH(CH₂CH₃)CH₂CH₃ is:
x: Every longest chain through the branch point has five carbons, with an ethyl group on the middle carbon, C-3. 3-methylhexane has the same formula, C₇H₁₆, but is a different isomer.

q: The ease of dehydration of alcohols with concentrated H₂SO₄ follows the order:
x: Tertiary alcohols lose water most easily and need the mildest conditions; primary alcohols such as ethanol need the strongest heating.

q: The IUPAC name of CH₃CH₂C≡CCH(CH₃)CH₃ is:
x: The main chain has six carbons and the triple bond is at carbon 3 from either end, so the tie is broken by giving the methyl group the lower number: 2-methylhex-3-yne. Hept-3-yne is the straight-chain isomer, a different compound.

q: A student names a compound "2-ethylbutane". The correct IUPAC name of this compound is:
x: Counting through the ethyl group gives a longer chain of five carbons with a methyl on C-3, so the compound is 3-methylpentane. An ethyl group on C-2 always means the longest chain was missed.

q: Butan-2-ol, CH₃CH(OH)CH₂CH₃, is dehydrated with concentrated H₂SO₄. The major product is:
x: By Saytzeff's rule, H is removed mainly from the β-carbon with fewer hydrogens, giving the more substituted alkene CH₃CH=CHCH₃. But-1-ene is the minor product, and 2-methylpropene would need a branched chain.

q: The IUPAC name of CH₂=CH–C≡CH (vinylacetylene) is:
x: Either numbering gives the multiple bonds locants 1 and 3; when there is such a tie, the double bond gets the lower number, so the name is but-1-en-3-yne. The ending is always '-en-…-yne', never '-yn-…-ene'.

q: The correct IUPAC name of CH₃CH(CH₃)CH(C₂H₅)CH₂CH₂CH₃ is:
x: The six-carbon chain is numbered to give the lowest locants (2 and 3, not 4 and 5), and the substituents are written in alphabetical order, so ethyl comes before methyl.

q: 2-bromo-2-methylpropane, (CH₃)₃CBr, is heated with alcoholic KOH. The organic product is:
x: HBr is eliminated to give (CH₃)₂C=CH₂, 2-methylpropene; all three β-carbons are the same, so only this alkene forms. The alcohol would form with aqueous KOH, not alcoholic KOH.

q: The IUPAC name of CH₃CH₂C≡CH is:
x: The chain has four carbons and is numbered from the end nearer the triple bond, so the triple bond starts at carbon 1: but-1-yne. Numbering from the other end (but-3-yne) gives a higher number, and the -ene ending is for a C=C bond.

q: The alkyl group (CH₃)₃C– is called:
x: In (CH₃)₃C– the carbon that attaches to the chain is bonded to three other carbons, so it is a tertiary (tert-) butyl group. Isobutyl is (CH₃)₂CHCH₂– and isopropyl is (CH₃)₂CH–.

q: Dehydration of ethanol and dehydrohalogenation of bromoethane are both examples of:
x: In both, a small molecule (H₂O or HBr) is removed from neighbouring carbons and a double bond forms. Addition is the reverse process.

q: 2-Methylbutane, (CH₃)₂CHCH₂CH₃, is chlorinated in sunlight. How many structurally different monochloro products are possible?
x: The molecule has four kinds of hydrogen: the two equivalent CH₃ groups on C-2, the H on C-2, the CH₂ hydrogens on C-3 and the end CH₃ (C-4). Each gives a different monochloroalkane, so 4. Counting the two methyl groups on C-2 separately gives the tempting 5.

q: Which equation is a chain-propagation step in the free-radical chlorination of methane?
x: A propagation step uses one radical and makes another, so the chain continues: Cl• takes an H atom from CH₄, giving HCl and CH₃•. Splitting Cl₂ is initiation and joining two radicals is termination, the usual mix-ups. The step giving H• is not observed.

q: A concentrated aqueous solution of sodium propanoate, CH₃CH₂COONa, is electrolysed (Kolbe's method). The alkane formed at the anode is:
x: At the anode each propanoate ion loses an electron and CO₂, giving an ethyl radical; two ethyl radicals join: 2CH₃CH₂COO⁻ → CH₃CH₂CH₂CH₃ + 2CO₂ + 2e⁻. Taking one ethyl group only gives the tempting ethane; ethane forms from soda-lime decarboxylation, not from Kolbe electrolysis.

q: A mixture of bromomethane and bromoethane is heated with sodium in dry ether (Wurtz reaction). Which alkane is NOT formed?
x: Sodium joins any two alkyl groups: CH₃ + CH₃ gives ethane, CH₃ + C₂H₅ gives propane and C₂H₅ + C₂H₅ gives butane. Pentane would need a C₂ and a C₃ group, and no propyl halide is present. Students who think a mixed Wurtz gives only the cross product miss that ethane and butane also form.

q: Sodium butanoate, CH₃CH₂CH₂COONa, is heated with soda lime (NaOH + CaO). The alkane formed is:
x: Soda lime removes the –COONa group as Na₂CO₃ and puts H in its place, so the chain loses one carbon: CH₃CH₂CH₂COONa + NaOH → CH₃CH₂CH₃ + Na₂CO₃. Forgetting that the carboxyl carbon leaves gives butane.

q: A mixture of methane and chlorine does not react in the dark at room temperature but reacts readily in sunlight. The reason is that light:
o: Breaks C–H bonds heterolytically to form CH₃⁺ ions
Ionises chlorine to Cl⁺ and Cl⁻, which attack methane
Raises the temperature enough for methane to decompose
Breaks Cl–Cl bonds homolytically to form chlorine free radicals
x: Light energy is absorbed by Cl₂, whose bond (about 242 kJ mol⁻¹) is much weaker than C–H; it splits evenly into two Cl• radicals that start the chain. The reaction is radical, not ionic, so the options with ions are the tempting slips from electrophilic chemistry.

q: An alkane of molar mass 72 g mol⁻¹ gives only one monochloro product on free-radical chlorination. The alkane is:
x: CₙH₂ₙ₊₂ = 72 gives 14n + 2 = 72, n = 5, so the alkane is C₅H₁₂. In 2,2-dimethylpropane, C(CH₃)₄, all 12 hydrogens are equivalent, so only one monochloro product forms; pentane gives 3 and 2-methylbutane 4. 2,2-Dimethylbutane is C₆H₁₄ (86 g mol⁻¹), tempting if the mass is not checked.

q: Propene reacts with hydrogen bromide in the absence of peroxides. The major product is:
x: H⁺ adds to the CH₂ end so that the more stable secondary carbocation CH₃CH⁺CH₃ forms; Br⁻ then joins C-2 (Markovnikov's rule). 1-Bromopropane is the anti-Markovnikov product, formed only with peroxides.

q: Propene reacts with hydrogen bromide in the presence of an organic peroxide. The major product is:
x: Peroxides make the addition go by free radicals (the peroxide or Kharasch effect): Br• adds to the CH₂ end to give the more stable secondary radical, and H then goes to C-2, so the product is anti-Markovnikov CH₃CH₂CH₂Br. Applying Markovnikov's rule regardless of the peroxide gives 2-bromopropane.

q: An alkene C₅H₁₀ is treated with ozone and the ozonide is decomposed with zinc and water. The products are propanone and ethanal. The alkene is:
x: Ozonolysis cuts the C=C and puts C=O on each carbon. Joining the carbonyl carbons of (CH₃)₂C=O and CH₃CH=O gives (CH₃)₂C=CHCH₃, 2-methylbut-2-ene. 2-Methylbut-1-ene would give butanone and methanal, and pent-2-ene ethanal and propanal, the usual slips from misplacing the double bond.

q: Ethene is passed through cold, dilute alkaline KMnO₄ solution (Baeyer's reagent). The purple colour disappears and the organic product is:
x: Cold dilute alkaline permanganate adds two –OH groups across the double bond: CH₂=CH₂ + H₂O + [O] → HOCH₂CH₂OH, and MnO₄⁻ is reduced to brown MnO₂. Ethanoic acid or further breakdown needs hot, concentrated or acidic permanganate, the tempting slip.

q: In the electrophilic addition of HBr to ethene, the first step is:
o: Br⁻ attacks one carbon, giving a carbanion
H⁺ from HBr bonds to one carbon using the π electrons, giving the carbocation CH₃CH₂⁺
A bromine free radical adds to one carbon
H and Br add to the two carbons at the same moment, with no intermediate
x: The electron-rich π bond attacks the electrophile H⁺ (HBr is polarised H^δ+–Br^δ−), forming CH₃CH₂⁺; Br⁻ then joins the carbocation in the second, fast step. Picking Br⁻ first confuses nucleophile and electrophile; the radical path occurs only with peroxides.

q: Propene is absorbed in cold concentrated sulphuric acid and the product is then warmed with water. The alcohol formed is:
x: H⁺ adds to the CH₂ end (Markovnikov), and HSO₄⁻ joins C-2 to give CH₃CH(OSO₃H)CH₃; hydrolysis replaces –OSO₃H with –OH, giving CH₃CH(OH)CH₃. Putting the group on the end carbon (anti-Markovnikov) gives the tempting propan-1-ol.

q: Ethyne reacts with sodium metal to give hydrogen and sodium ethynide (acetylide), but ethene does not. The reason is that the carbon bonded to hydrogen in ethyne is:
o: sp² hybridised with 33% s character, which makes its C–H bond weakest
sp³ hybridised, so its C–H bond is the longest
Bonded to more hydrogen atoms than the carbons in ethene
sp hybridised with 50% s character, so it holds the C–H bonding electrons closer and the H is released as H⁺ more easily
x: More s character keeps electrons nearer the nucleus, so an sp carbon is more electronegative; the C≡C–H hydrogen is weakly acidic and the ethynide ion is relatively stable. Ethene's carbons are sp² (33% s), the tempting slip, and ethyne has fewer H atoms, not more.

q: Which reagent gives a precipitate with but-1-yne but not with but-2-yne?
x: Only a terminal alkyne has an acidic ≡C–H; but-1-yne gives a white precipitate of silver butynide with ammoniacal AgNO₃, while but-2-yne has no such hydrogen. Bromine water and KMnO₄ react with both triple bonds, so they cannot tell the two apart, and hydrogenation gives no precipitate.

q: Propyne, CH₃C≡CH, is passed into dilute sulphuric acid containing mercury(II) sulphate at about 75 °C. The final organic product is:
x: Water adds by Markovnikov's rule, putting –OH on the middle carbon to give the enol CH₃C(OH)=CH₂, which rearranges at once to the ketone CH₃COCH₃. Anti-Markovnikov addition would give propanal, and stopping at an alcohol ignores the enol–keto change; only ethyne gives an aldehyde (ethanal) this way.

q: Ethyne is made by adding water to calcium carbide: CaC₂ + 2H₂O → Ca(OH)₂ + C₂H₂. What mass of CaC₂ is needed to give 11.2 dm³ of ethyne at STP? (Molar volume 22.4 dm³ mol⁻¹)
x: 11.2 ÷ 22.4 = 0.5 mol C₂H₂, which needs 0.5 mol CaC₂ (1 : 1). Mr of CaC₂ = 40 + 24 = 64, so mass = 0.5 × 64 = 32 g. Using 1 mol (forgetting to convert the volume) gives 64 g.

q: 1,2-Dibromoethane, BrCH₂CH₂Br, is heated with excess alcoholic KOH so that two molecules of HBr are removed from each molecule. The final organic product is:
x: The first elimination gives bromoethene, CH₂=CHBr; the second removes another HBr to give HC≡CH. Bromoethene is the tempting answer if only one HBr is removed; ethane-1,2-diol would come from aqueous KOH, which substitutes instead of eliminating.

q: Ethyne reacts with two moles of hydrogen bromide. The final product is:
x: The first HBr gives CH₂=CHBr. In the second addition H goes to the CH₂ end and Br to the carbon already carrying Br (Markovnikov's rule; that carbocation is stabilised by the bromine), giving CH₃CHBr₂. Putting one Br on each carbon gives the tempting 1,2-dibromoethane, which is the product of Br₂ with ethene.

q: Ethyne is passed through a red-hot iron tube. Three molecules join together to form:
x: Polymerisation of three HC≡CH molecules gives the ring C₆H₆, benzene. Cyclohexane, C₆H₁₂, would need extra hydrogen, and hex-1-yne is not a ring, the usual slips when only the carbon count is checked.
